title: Why I never deload (and why you shouldn't either)
summary: NH explains why he never takes powerlifting-style deload weeks: he trains 2-3 hours daily within 0-2 RIR, takes only Sundays off and never cuts load. He argues bodybuilders should manage fatigue continuously through autoregulated 'bodybuilding deloads' built into frequency, evolving rep/set schemes and exercise rotations, using a bucket metaphor for recovery.
claims: NH never takes a week off, never deliberately reduces the load on his lifts, takes no rest days except Sundays, and never trains further than 1-2 reps from failure
He trains 2-3 hours every day at or near failure on every exercise yet keeps progressing year-round without deloads
Recovery only matters if real training preceded it; many lifters allocate rest disproportionate to the stimulus they actually applied
Most people overestimate the muscle damage they cause and so inflate how much rest and recovery they need
The training must dictate the deload, never the reverse; planning a deload first and fitting training around it is reverse engineering at its worst
Fixing a one-week deload and then a five-week block before it suits powerlifters, but bodybuilders should first set optimal work and then see what recovery it needs
A deload has two purposes: recovery and preparing for peak performance; the peaking half is useless for bodybuilders, who want stable, slowly progressing strength rather than peak strength
Bodybuilding strength progresses more slowly than powerlifting strength because the goal is different, not because the lifts differ
Full week-off deloads have mostly disappeared from YouTube fitness; most now train with submaximal loads, which makes sense for strength but does almost nothing for hypertrophy
Powerlifting tools like RIR sandbagging and speed pulls at about 40% of 1RM prepare for peak strength but are pointless for bodybuilders
Reduce the workload before the deload week so a deload never becomes necessary, rather than reducing load during a deload week
Never plan on a deload week to save you; knowing one is coming makes people overzealous with volume or intensity beforehand
Deload weeks lose quality tonnage, create performance instability you must rebuild, and encourage PR-chasing at the expense of muscle damage
Example: rather than 295 lb then a week off to hit a 315 lb squat PR, going 295, 297-298, 300 accumulates more tonnage and more muscle than the PR, which is usually only a 1RM
A muscle doesn't need a full week off; it needs around 48 hours, up to 72, and even a fully trashed muscle is fresh again in 4-5 days
A deload can only restore a muscle to its normal capacity (100), never beyond it, so emptying it fully before a deload gains nothing
Bucket metaphor: training empties the bucket, rest refills it; dropping to 40 and refilling to 100 twice (120 points) beats one 100-to-0 crash and a full refill
The water at the top of the bucket is quality tonnage, far from the baseline where a muscle can barely function; never empty it to total-crash baseline
Emptying the bucket down to near exhaustion before a deload is usually done with junk volume, not hard sets of 3-5 reps
Taking only 30-40% off the bucket each session is safer, promotes quality tonnage, lower injury rates and the ability to train frequently
His approach is autoregulation, a 'bodybuilding deload' that keeps each muscle stimulated continuously rather than letting it fully recover
A muscle doesn't need to recover to 100% before retraining; 90-95% still works, and waiting for full recovery pushes people towards bro splits
Training a muscle before it has fully recovered is not wasted; it just adds fatigue and lengthens the next recovery, a problem only if done constantly
Training a muscle on consecutive days (e.g. 90%, 80%, 70% Mon-Wed, then rest till Saturday) is a valid alternative to one big session
Small doses like a few pull-ups for the lats take only a little off the top, recover fast and can be repeated daily
Retrain a muscle whenever it is ready again rather than waiting until it is fully recovered; a muscle left dormant once recovered stagnates or regresses
Movement patterns share neural patterns, so you don't need to bench every other day; any press every other day maintains it
A muscle hit hard on Monday should not be hit hard again on Tuesday
He never takes weight off the bar: if he deadlifts 460 he never drops to 440, because that is regression; he controls intensity through reps and sets instead
Dropping reps on a strength lift is fine only if the lost tonnage is made up elsewhere in the program, e.g. back-off sets
Use evolving reps and sets on the strength lift plus flexible back-off sets so tonnage stays constant and strength progresses steadily with no deloads
Example: main lift at 1-3 sets of 2-4 reps; on a weak day do one set of 2, then follow with a same-pattern exercise for 3-4 sets of 8-12 to keep tonnage
Going to failure guarantees high-intensity, quality tonnage unless the rep range is ridiculous like 35 reps
Squatting to failure daily drains capacity (100, 75, 55...) so by day four the loads are so far off that it becomes junk volume; junk volume also comes from poor scheduling
Exercise rotations are his main volume-control tool: have interchangeable exercises for different muscle groups that can be switched in or out each session
He trains upper body every two days with four upper-day iterations, each including a biceps exercise that can be used or skipped as needed
Advanced programs become complex but not complicated; he hasn't looked at his written program in a year because it is ingrained
Put a quad option on every lower day; skip it if quads are at 65%, use it to take them from 95% to 70% if they are fresh
Picture body parts flashing red when they need work and green when they need recovery, and let the program respond
On a day where chest needs rest, reduce it to a single evolving-rep set or rotate it out entirely
This autoregulated system suits more advanced lifters who know their bodies; beginners should work towards it gradually
Novice programs should be minimalistic enough that deloads are unnecessary; a novice who needs a deload is doing too much
Bodybuilding deloads are non-arbitrary: if the biceps are fresh despite a planned rotation, he trains them anyway
Scheduled deload weeks taken when not fatigued are a complete waste of time
Junk volume isn't necessarily bad, but quality volume is always better and this system reduces junk volume to nearly zero
The idea that muscles need a week or two of inactivity to resensitize is nonsense; he resensitizes via rotations such as switching dumbbell pullovers to cable pullovers or changing the angle
Rotations should never be scheduled (e.g. every two weeks) nor triggered just by a plateau; use them when the muscle needs it
A plateau means the weight is now maximally challenging for this period; repeating it still produces hard sets and quality tonnage
Strength progression matters because it raises tonnage, but the end goal is quality tonnage
Bodybuilding deloads are micro-blocks built into each day: the grey deload block is split into switchable patches spread across the week
Rigid hard blocks contradict the stability muscle growth needs
Volume, intensity and frequency are the holy trinity of bodybuilding and are really one thing: tools to manage fatigue
exercises: never take weight off the bar; vary reps/sets instead
keeps strength carrying over to hip hinges and accessories
a few sets daily to take a little off the top
fast-recovering lat stimulus that can be repeated every day
switch tool or angle when you stop feeling it
resensitizes the muscle without a break
3-4 sets of 8-12 after the strength work, same movement pattern
make up tonnage lost when the main lift is reduced
